title: Build the glasses
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Whose opinion about your idea do you give the most weight?

One of the hardest things as an entrepreneur is keeping your convictions when everybody tells you: you cannot build rockets, you cannot do this, Jose said. If you are doing something new, something nobody has done, you are going to suffer self-doubt.

His conviction is unwavering. You have to have that makeup, that inner fortitude. If you don't have it, you better build it, because people will tell you you're crazy. Nobody else can judge that for you. Only you can judge it for yourself.

He said he has suffered that in tiny ways compared to these people: people close to him thought he had gone off the deep end, and he hears from them: why can't you just sit still? You cannot let that rocky road take you away.

groups.heading: When people don't see your vision

lines.text: A student asked: when people aren't seeing your vision, what helps you see things through, or know when it's time to adjust?

Jose said it depends on the business. Sometimes you can show the data: this is my vision and this is the evidence. But what if you don't have data? He buys real estate in very remote places, with no comparables within a hundred miles, and people say: we may as well be on Mars.

So he shows a small proof of concept: what are the characteristics of this land that other land doesn't have, and what market is under it? If you don't have the data, build the criteria for people to see what you're seeing. Don't expect them to see it right away.
It's like the movies in 3D, he said. You take people to your movie and give them the glasses. You build the glasses of what they are going to see, and you get better and better and test it.
Can you be wrong? Yes, he said: you can believe in something that doesn't have value, or it does but you cannot realistically monetize it. A student added: monetize in different ways.

I've run into businesses where the idea was brilliant and everybody got it, he said. But nobody saw the learning curve of what it takes for a company to adapt to the new technology, and the millions of dollars it took for people to change their behavior.
People naturally resist new technology. Adopting a large software system could take two years before the company runs on all cylinders, he said. Who is going to pick up that bill?
What glasses do you hand someone so they can see what you see?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write one conviction you hold that others doubt.
Write what evidence supports it, and what you lack.
Write the small proof you could show.
Write the glasses someone needs to see what you see.
Write who pays for the learning curve if people must change.

check.q: What did Jose say you can do if you have no data?
choices: Build the criteria so people can see what you see

check.q: What image did Jose use for showing people your vision?
What did nobody see in the brilliant ideas Jose mentioned?
choices: The learning curve and the cost of changing behavior

recap: Hold your convictions. Build the glasses. Price the learning curve.
